title: What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.
ai_summary: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed . Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter .

title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
ai_summary: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models . We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression . We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for large language models .

title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
abstract: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.
ai_summary: Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT) unify social media profiling . The two disciplines evolved separately into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle .

title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
abstract: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.
ai_summary: G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal . The same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling .

title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
ai_summary: CellTrack-Bench assesses Vision-Language Models' cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers . The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell- tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems .

title: Squaring-the-Sphere: Distortion-Free and Seamless Panorama Generation via CubeAtlas
abstract: Generating 360-degree panoramas requires both local perspective fidelity and global spherical continuity. Existing representations face a trade-off: equirectangular projection (ERP) enables seamless panorama modeling but suffers from severe distortion and a domain gap to pre-trained image generators, whereas cubemaps preserve perspective geometry but often produce inconsistent faces and visible seams. We present Squaring-the-Sphere, a panoramic image generation framework built on a novel representation CubeAtlas, which unfolds all cubemap faces into a single compact canvas. By arranging orientation-aligned, rotated polar regions alongside the equatorial faces, this representation preserves the perspective geometry of cubemaps while organizing the cross-face relationships required for seamless panorama assembly. It further enables a pretrained diffusion transformer to model the complete panorama jointly in a single pass, without altering the backbone architecture or positional encoding. While CubeAtlas has a token count comparable to ERP, its structured layout makes many dense attention interactions unnecessary. We therefore introduce a layout-aware sparse attention mask that preserves the interactions required for panorama continuity while removing geometrically irrelevant token pairs. As a result, CubeAtlas achieves better quality than ERP modeling with lower attention computation. Furthermore, we introduce a training-free super-resolution technique and a fusion scheme that enhance fine details in distortion-free perspective space before achieving the final ERP panorama. Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves geometric fidelity, cross-view consistency, and high-resolution visual quality over previous methods.
ai_summary: Squaring-the-Sphere is a panoramic image generation framework built on a novel representation CubeAtlas . It unfolds all cubemap faces into a single compact canvas . It further enables a pretrained diffusion transformer to model the complete panorama jointly in a single pass .

title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Online Policy Distillation (OPD) often outperforms offline methods such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) by training on trajectories sampled directly from the student. However, standard OPD trains the student to follow the teacher at every state of the trajectory, assuming that teacher guidance is always beneficial. We instead distinguish between what the teacher prefers and what actually helps the current student succeed. We introduce Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation (AOPD), which weights teacher actions by their counterfactual advantage under the student. Teacher actions that improve the student's expected outcome are reinforced, while those that do not are downweighted. Directly computing these advantages requires trying alternative teacher actions at each step and running new rollouts from each. Instead, we show that the AOPD objective can be estimated using only standard student rollouts and their terminal rewards. Our estimator uses teacher importance weights on the student-sampled actions to provide unbiased advantage-weighted supervision, without any additional rollouts or reward evaluations. This allows AOPD to focus teacher supervision on actions that help the current student while preserving the rollout efficiency of standard OPD. Experiments on math, coding, and Medqa show gains over distillation and RL baselines in both external-teacher and self-distillation settings.
ai_summary: Online Policy Distillation (OPD) often outperforms offline methods such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) by training on trajectories sampled directly from the student . We instead distinguish between what the teacher prefers and what actually helps the current student succeed .

title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks
abstract: \emph{Continuous-space} attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs by sampling or optimizing over a low-dimensional Gaussian latent space and decoding it to text through a \emph{random mapping} and nearest-token lookup. Because the random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural, and as such easily detectable through input guardrails, and the risk estimates they yield are not grounded in natural prompts. In this paper, we demonstrate that the same continuous latent-space framework can be coupled directly to a learned generative distribution over language, a continuous diffusion language model (dLLM), which removes the artificial random mapping while preserving the standard-Gaussian latent formulation and the downstream sampling or optimization procedure. We evaluate this approach under two settings: sampling-based estimation using \emph{RareTrap} and optimization-based search using \emph{ThinkTrap}. We find that character-level perplexity drops from $10^3$--$10^7$ to 3--5 in RareTrap and from 20--28 to 4.3--5.4 in ThinkTrap. We also find that model risk estimates can differ by an order of magnitude across the two mappings.
ai_summary: \emph{Continuous-space. attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs . The random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural .

title: Contestable Agents for Data Governance: Recording Human Stewardship of AI-Generated Metadata Across Structured and Unstructured Systems
abstract: Industrial organizations hold operational knowledge in structured records, such as telemetry, point lists, and transactions, and in unstructured sources, such as manuals, service notes, communications, and inspection reports. Governance programs often manage these sources separately. Classifying, linking, and documenting them depends on a small group of employees with deep domain knowledge. Agents built on large language models can propose metadata, cite documents, and flag quality issues, but unreviewed proposals can spread errors into downstream systems. A perfunctory approval leaves no record of what a reviewer checked. We present contestable governance: specialist agents produce scored, cited arguments for disputed metadata decisions; a steward can accept, reject, modify, or add arguments before commit; and a governance record retains the evidence, interventions, and outcome. A versioned domain glossary supplies model-specific terms and acronym definitions to the agents. We describe the workflow, a triage path that reserves full argumentation for uncertain proposals while preserving review before commit, the scoring and record models, and a gate that controls which verified decisions become precedent. Two HVAC use cases illustrate the pattern: point classification using Brick Schema class labels, supported by an open reference implementation, and an illustrative warranty failure-mode decision linking claim fields and telemetry to service notes and revisioned bulletins.
ai_summary: Industrial organizations hold operational knowledge in structured records, such as telemetry, point lists, and transactions . Governance programs often manage these sources separately . Agents built on large language models can propose metadata, cite documents, and flag quality issues .

title: CAMGen: A Core Change-Aware Multi-View Framework for Commit Message Generation
abstract: Commit messages help developers understand code changes and support software maintenance. Recent approaches use repository context to improve commit message generation (CMG) with large language models (LLMs). However, existing CMG methods provide limited support for understanding how local edits affect functionality jointly implemented by multiple code entities. This functional understanding is essential for generating commit messages that explain the main change and its impact. To address this problem, we propose CAMGen, a core change-aware multi-view commit message generation framework that incorporates functional context into generation. CAMGen identifies core entities that represent the primary change intent. It then forms candidate functional units through repository-wide semantic clustering and uses those containing the core entities to construct a Functional Semantic View. This view supplies semantic context for interpreting the affected functionality. CAMGen also uses context provided by the Structural Dependency View and the Historical Exemplar View. The context from all three views is then provided to the LLM together with the code diff to guide CMG. The experimental results show that CAMGen outperforms representative CMG baselines across three programming languages. Human evaluation further shows that CAMGen generates more complete commit messages with clearer explanations of change rationale and impact. These results demonstrate the value of functional context and complementary repository information for CMG.
ai_summary: Commit messages help developers understand code changes and support software maintenance . We propose CAMGen, a core change-aware multi-view commit message generation framework . CAMGen identifies core entities that represent the primary change intent . It then forms candidate functional units through repository-wide semantic clustering .

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability
abstract: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Existing theoretical analyses often rely on specific model or task structures and offer limited insight into how iterative optimization affects forgetting. To address this gap, we develop an algorithmic stability framework for expected population forgetting under SGD without prescribing a particular model architecture. Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. To bound the generalization gaps, we track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks. We consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules. Comparing the two decaying schedules allows us to characterize how restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects the propagation of historical sample perturbations. For empirical forgetting, we derive bounds for all three schedules by retaining cumulative gradient alignment along the optimization trajectory, without requiring convexity. Combining these results yields upper bounds on expected forgetting that capture the effects of training set size, the number of updates per task, the total number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.

We track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks . title: Shift-aware score transport for privacy auditing without retraining
abstract: Privacy auditing empirically assesses privacy leakage by using membership inference attacks to establish lower bounds on privacy loss. We consider an observational auditing setting in which the auditor cannot insert canaries, control data inclusion, or retrain the target model, and must instead rely on fixed sets of known members and non-members. This setting is relevant for large deployed models or when retraining is restricted by computational or access constraints. In this case, non-members available for auditing may differ in distribution from the training data, causing membership-inference scores to be skewed due to the distribution shift. We address this problem by estimating the counterfactual in-distribution non-member score distribution using the available out-of-distribution (OOD) non-members. Our proposed method learns the relationship between data representations and membership-inference scores from OOD non-members and transports it to the target covariate distribution. Because this transport may become unreliable under extrapolation or imperfect conditional invariance, we further introduce a conservative correction calibrated directly to the nominal transported privacy level. We construct controlled calibration tasks from the available non-member data to estimate how representation-space displacement inflates the audit, and use this estimate to correct the transport-induced audit error. Across multiple datasets with distribution shifts, our method yields substantially more stable privacy estimates while retaining tighter lower bounds than baselines.
ai_summary: Privacy auditing assesses privacy leakage by using membership inference attacks to establish lower bounds on privacy loss . We consider an observational auditing setting in which the auditor cannot insert canaries, control data inclusion, or retrain the target model . This setting is relevant for large deployed models or when retraining is restricted by computational or access constraints.

title: Same Luck, Different Choice: Twin-World Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning rewards a complete episode, yet the policy needs credit for every decision inside it. Counterfactual branching estimates this credit by re-running the episode after an alternative decision, but the branch draws its sampling noise independently of the factual episode, so the outcome difference mixes the effect of the decision with the luck of everything that follows. We observe that in agentic search the retriever, the corpus, and the grader are deterministic, so an episode is a deterministic function of the policy's decisions and its sampling noise. Twin worlds are therefore realizable: the same noise, a different decision. We introduce TWICE (TWIn-world Credit Estimation), which keys the Gumbel noise of every token by turn and line, rolls out counterfactual twins that inherit the factual episode's downstream noise, and turns their paired outcome differences into turn-level advantages for policy-gradient updates on actor-sampled trajectories; only the actor is deployed. Twin credit is unbiased for any coupling quality, its variance is that of an independent counterfactual scaled by $1-ρ$, where $ρ$ is the twins' outcome correlation, and under coupling the number of rollouts needed to resolve an advantage of size $Δ$ falls from $Θ(Δ^{-2})$ to $Θ(Δ^{-1})$. A square-root rule spends the twin budget where outcomes are predicted to disagree per unit cost. On seven question-answering benchmarks, TWICE improves the average exact match of GRPO by 5.3 and 4.5 points on Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, outperforms tree-search and counterfactual-branching baselines, and uses 68% fewer auxiliary tokens than VinePPO.

title: PYTHIA, a transferable machine learning framework for simultaneous defect and adsorption site optimization
abstract: Machine learning has permeated material optimization, providing high value. In this paper we extend the applicability of machine learning to novel and understudied materials through the PYTHIA (Probabilistic Yet Transferable Hierarchical Interaction Architecture) framework. Pythia utilizes two of the most powerful machine learning concepts, foundational models and transfer learning. We employ a complex foundational model trained on a large dataset of chemically similar molecules, on a target that is physically close to our prediction target. Then, we freeze the weights and perform subspace alignment with the use of a transformer layer and add uncertainty quantification with gaussian processes. title: A systematic benchmarking pipeline for demand forecasting and inventory-aware supply chain decision support.
abstract: Demand forecasting has been shown to be one of the key facilitators of successful supply chain and inventory management. In this work, we introduce a benchmarking pipeline for demand forecasting in retail that includes data preprocessing, comparative benchmarking of different machine learning/deep learning (ML/DL) approaches, and decision-focused evaluation. Unlike other works that compare predictive performance of ML/DL models and end there, our pipeline links reproducible ML/DL benchmarking and decision-focused evaluation through cost of inventory management in order to derive costs from forecasting error/bias. We also present a scalability study on another retail dataset. Several standard forecasting models, such as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), CNN-LSTM, and XGBoost, are compared using a unified experimental pipeline on benchmark retail datasets. The experimental results reveal that while the deep learning models efficiently identify temporal dependencies, tree-based ensemble algorithms, especially XGBoost, consistently deliver better results in terms of forecasting accuracy on structured retail demand datasets. A scalability case study on the Rossmann Store Sales benchmark evaluates the top-performing model on a larger, richer dataset. Moreover, the study shows the connection between forecast accuracy and the subsequent inventory performance by performing a cost-based evaluation of inventory outcomes of forecasts made using various models.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in exercise and physical activity for public health: a scoping review.
abstract: Physical activity and exercise are important components of public health strategies for preventing and managing chronic conditions and promoting health and quality of life. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have broadened its applications in this field, from personalized interventions and monitoring to risk prediction, professional decision support, and planning. This scoping review aimed to map the literature on AI-based exercise and physical activity applications from a public health perspective, characterize their functional roles, and examine the scope and maturity of the research. This scoping review followed the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and JBI methodological guidance. Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed were searched for eligible studies published between 2015 and 2025. Two Reviewers independently conducted title and abstract screening and full-text assessment, resolving disagreements by consensus. Of 612 records identified, 601 remained after duplicate removal and 24 studies met the eligibility criteria. The included studies were characterized by publication year, country, study design, AI technology and function, and stage of evidence development. Key findings were synthesized across the identified functional categories. Among the included studies, publication activity was highest in 2024, while China accounted for the largest number of studies. Five functional categories were identified: Intervention Delivery or Adaptation, Monitoring or Assessment, Prediction or Risk Stratification, Professional Decision Support, and System and Environmental Planning. Research maturity differed across these functions. Technical development and validation studies often reported promising performance, whereas intervention findings were less consistent and did not always show additional benefit over comparison conditions. Many studies remained at the model-development, technical-validation, feasibility, or pilot stage. AI is being used across several functions in exercise and physical activity, although evidence of consistent clinical or public health benefit remains limited. Current findings support its complementary use in personalization, monitoring, prediction, and professional decision support; the available findings do not justify autonomous clinical decision-making. Further controlled studies, external validation, longer follow-up, and real-world evaluation are needed to establish whether technical capabilities translate into sustained physical activity and meaningful health outcomes. Implementation should also account for professional oversight, data protection, and the needs of diverse populations.

title: Establishing standardized evaluation protocols for peptide-target interaction prediction: the PTI-TAPE consensus framework eDelphi.
abstract: Computational peptide-target interaction (PTI) prediction has advanced rapidly as a tool for drug discovery, yet the field lacks agreed evaluation standards. Discrepancies in metrics, negative sampling strategies, and dataset construction across publications currently render cross-study comparisons methodologically intractable, ultimately impeding the clinical translation of therapeutic peptides. To resolve this, we present PTI-TAPE (Peptide-Target Interaction-Tasks Assessing Peptide Engagement), a standardised benchmarking framework developed via a structured three-round eDelphi consensus study with 15 international experts spanning computational biology, machine learning, and regulatory science. Operating under a robust consensus threshold (>80% agreement), the panel established 26 definitive standards across eight domains, governed by the new STRIDE (Standardisation, Transparency, Representativeness, Integration, Discovery, Evidence) framework. Key outcomes include mandating specific primary metrics for affinity and structure, enforcing a tiered negative sampling hierarchy that prioritizes experimental non-binders, and requiring mandatory temporal dataset splits. By providing a unified reporting checklist, benchmark specifications, and a biennial governance structure, PTI-TAPE ensures reproducible evaluation and fair method comparison, bridging the gap between computational PTI predictions and genuine therapeutic benefit.

title: Sustainable high performance computing in the UK: a position paper on public investment, accountability, and the path to net zero.
abstract: The UK invests significantly in High-Performance Computing (HPC), yet has no coherent national strategy that addresses sustainability, accountability, or long-term infrastructure planning. This paper proposes and promotes three key messages: first, that the return on public investment cannot be assessed without consistent public reporting on utilisation, research outputs, and cost-effectiveness for all publicly funded HPC systems; second, that publicly funded HPC systems should be subject to mandatory, standardised reporting on energy consumption, carbon emissions, with information on what happens when a system is decommissioned; and third, that the conflation of AI and HPC in UK policy is a strategic error. Instead, HPC is the underpinning infrastructure, and AI is one of many types of applications using that infrastructure, alongside numerical modelling and simulation. Treating AI and HPC as separate, competing workloads risks under-serving the wider research community that depends upon that shared infrastructure, resulting in a weakening rather than strengthening of the UK's national compute capability.

title: Phenotyping of AMI patients using machine learning: integration of clinical, metabolic, and behavioral features to identify high-risk "frailty-inflammation" phenotype.
abstract: Prognosis among patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) shows substantial heterogeneity, making precise identification of high-risk phenotypes essential for improving long-term outcomes. Machine learning techniques were used to identify such phenotypes by integrating multidimensional data and to examine their association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). A total of 1,139 patients with AMI were enrolled from the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University between March 2023 and June 2024. Multidimensional data, including clinical features, metabolic characteristics, and behavioral patterns, were collected. Phenotyping was performed using a hierarchical clustering algorithm. Associations between derived phenotypes and 1-year MACE were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariable Cox regression models. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values derived from an XGBoost model were used to quantify the contributions of individual variables to cluster assignment. This phenotype offers a comprehensive biological-functional-behavioral framework for risk stratification and may support early and precise clinical interventions to reduce long-term adverse outcomes. However, despite its potential clinical value, the current evidence is insufficient to support direct translation into routine clinical practice until independent cohort validation is performed. Explainable fine-grained feature enhancement framework for strawberry diagnostic decision making.
abstract: As the number of smart agricultural automation systems increases, accurate disease diagnosis is essential to maximize production efficiency. However, early-stage symptoms of strawberry diseases (e.g., Tipburn, Phytophthora blight, and Fusarium wilt) often manifest as low-contrast micro-symptoms that are visually similar to the inherent complex texture of strawberry leaves, leading to high technical difficulties in achieving an accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, providing an explanation for the diagnosis remains challenging, which hinders trust in field applications. We present EN-FDEA, a deep learning framework that integrates an EfficientNetV2 backbone with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) and a Fine-grained Discriminative Enhancement (FDEA) module combining depthwise separable convolution, parallel feature amplification, and channel recalibration, and we evaluate it together with a provenance audit of the corpus on which it is trained. Parsing the acquisition metadata embedded in every file name showed that the 1,000 abnormal images of each disease originate from only 33-73 individual plants, and that normal and abnormal images share no greenhouse; under the image-level cross-validation used in the original design, 91.9-99.8% of abnormal plants appear in both the training and the test partition of a fold. All results reported here are therefore obtained under plant-disjoint cross-validation with five random seeds, with a site-disjoint arm as the strictest comparison. Removing plant leakage lowers balanced accuracy by up to 0.082 and removing site overlap by up to 0.173. Under the leakage-free protocol, EN-FDEA performs comparably to, and not reliably better than, its EfficientNetV2 backbone (mean paired balanced-accuracy differences of -0.013 to +0.012 across datasets and conditions); the only Holm-corrected significant advantage is Phytophthora blight under overexposure (+0.012, p = 0.047). Forensic analysis further shows that the elevated performance previously observed under synthetic overexposure is a property of the transform: a logistic-regression classifier using only global exposure statistics reaches balanced accuracies of 0.81-0.92, and models trained on original images transfer poorly to synthetic overexposure while transferring well to genuinely over-illuminated frames selected from the corpus itself. We report explanation faithfulness, calibration, and measured deployment cost, and we state where the corpus structure, rather than the model, bounds what can be concluded. Code, split definitions, and per-image predictions are released so that every number can be regenerated.

title: Association of metabolic syndrome and its components with knee osteoarthritis in the older adults of Amirkola City.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis is a very common disease that leads to mobility disabilities in older adults. In recent years, a link between metabolic syndrome and knee osteoarthritis has been reported. However, there are conflicting findings regarding this association. Our study was conducted to investigate the relationship between metabolic syndrome and its components and knee osteoarthritis in the older adults of Amirkola City. In this case-control study, the diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis was based on the EULAR criteria. 590 older adults were examined in two groups of older adults with and without knee osteoarthritis. Both groups were compared on the frequency of metabolic syndrome and its components. Also, the variables of quadriceps femoris muscle strength, body mass index, physical activity level, and smoking were investigated as control variables between the two groups. Data was analyzed using SPSS 20 software and statistical tests of chi-square, t-test, and logistic regression. A significance level of p< 0.05 was considered. In this study, there was no significant relationship between knee osteoarthritis and metabolic syndrome (OR = 1.38, CI = 0.98-1.93, P = .06). Among the components of metabolic syndrome, waist circumference (P = 0.004) and blood pressure (P = 0.007) had a significant relationship with knee osteoarthritis. The variables of quadriceps femoris muscle strength, physical activity level, and age had a significant effect on knee osteoarthritis. These findings show that knee osteoarthritis has no significant relationship with metabolic syndrome and its components, except for blood pressure and waist circumference.
